advisory.title: Quadratic parsing of nested image wikilinks with `ENABLE_WIKILINKS`
advisory.description:
With `Options::ENABLE_WIKILINKS`, handle_wikilink builds a wikilink's target
from the raw text of its body: scan_wikilink_pipe walks it looking for |, then
contains('\0') and from_replace_nuls walk it again.
Once a wikilink is created, disable_all_links only disables Link entries, so
every enclosing `![[` stays live on the wikilink stack.
On `![[![[![[…]]]]]]` each of those openers then resolves in turn and rescans
everything inside it, which is quadratic in the nesting depth.
The event count stays tiny, because in the unpiped case each enclosing image
replaces its body with a fresh text node, so all of that work is thrown away.

Applications that parse untrusted Markdown with `ENABLE_WIKILINKS` set,
including through `Options::all()`, are affected. The option is off by default.
Parsing without it is not affected.

The flaw was fixed in
[#1186](https://github.com/pulldown-cmark/pulldown-cmark/pull/1186) and
released in 0.13.6.

advisory.title: Exponential event growth with `ENABLE_WIKILINKS`
advisory.description:
When `Options::ENABLE_WIKILINKS` is enabled, a wikilink with a pipe separator
and empty display text, such as `[[a|]]`, leaks its child node's sibling chain
into the content that follows it. Each such link roughly doubles the number of
events the parser yields for the rest of the document, so output grows
exponentially with input size: 16 repetitions of `[[a|]] ` (112 bytes) yield
327,676 events, where the fixed parser yields 65. A document of a few kilobytes
is enough to exhaust memory in a process that collects the events or renders
them to HTML.

Applications that parse untrusted Markdown with `ENABLE_WIKILINKS` set,
including through `Options::all()`, are affected. The option is off by default.
Parsing without it is not affected.

The flaw was fixed in
[#1102](https://github.com/pulldown-cmark/pulldown-cmark/pull/1102) and
released in 0.13.5.

advisory.title: `ttf-parser` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The author of `ttf-parser` has stated that the crate is unmaintained and will not receive further fixes (see the referenced issue).

## Alternative(s)

- [`skrifa`](https://crates.io/crates/skrifa), an actively maintained TrueType and OpenType font parsing crate, part of the Google Fonts "oxidize" (`fontations`) project.

advisory.title: unsafe-libyaml is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The [repository](https://github.com/dtolnay/unsafe-libyaml) was archived by
its owner on 2024-03-25 and is read-only. The last release is 0.2.11
(March 2024).

`unsafe-libyaml` is a machine translation of libyaml's C code into unsafe
Rust (c2rust). Bugs found in it will not be fixed upstream. It is used by
`serde_yaml` (itself deprecated) and by forks such as `serde_yaml_ng`.

## Alternatives

Consider a YAML parser written in safe Rust, for example:

- [saphyr](https://crates.io/crates/saphyr) ([serde-saphyr](https://crates.io/crates/serde-saphyr) for serde users)
- [noyalib](https://crates.io/crates/noyalib)

advisory.title: xattr functions mark unwritten bytes as initialized when given a zero-length buffer
advisory.description:
The extended-attribute functions in `rustix::fs` (`getxattr`, `lgetxattr`, `fgetxattr`, `listxattr`, `llistxattr` and `flistxattr`) write into a `Buffer` and then mark as many bytes initialized as the system call reported. When the buffer has zero length, the operating system treats the call as a size query: it writes nothing and returns the size of the attribute value or of the name list. rustix still marked that many bytes as initialized.

Passing a `Vec` whose length equals its capacity through `spare_capacity` gives such a zero-length buffer, and rustix then set the vector's length past its capacity over memory that was never written. This is undefined behavior reachable from safe code. With an empty `&mut [MaybeUninit<u8>]` the call panics instead.

From 1.1.6 these functions return an empty result for a zero-length buffer, and new `getxattr_query`, `lgetxattr_query`, `fgetxattr_query`, `listxattr_query`, `llistxattr_query` and `flistxattr_query` functions return the size. The 0.38 series did not have the `Buffer` API and is not affected.

advisory.title: `AsyncFd::new` and related constructors violate I/O safety
advisory.description:
`tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd` provides safe constructors (`new`, `with_interest`, `try_new`, and `try_with_interest`) that accept any `T: AsRawFd` rather than requiring proof of ownership or validity of the file descriptor. Because `RawFd` implements `AsRawFd`, safe code can construct an `AsyncFd` from an arbitrary or closed file descriptor, or close/replace the underlying file descriptor while the `AsyncFd` is still alive.

This violates I/O safety in two ways:

1. `AsyncFd<T>` implements `AsFd` for all `T: AsRawFd` by calling `BorrowedFd::borrow_raw(self.as_raw_fd())`, allowing safe code to obtain an arbitrary `BorrowedFd<'_>` without owning the file descriptor.
2. Tokio's I/O driver stores a pointer to an internal allocation in the `epoll`/`kqueue` user data for registered file descriptors. If the underlying file descriptor is duplicated and then closed while an `AsyncFd` is alive, and the OS reuses that file descriptor number for a another IO resource on the same runtime, dropping the first `AsyncFd` deregisters the reused file descriptor number and frees the first while the original file description remains registered in `epoll`, leading to a use-after-free when a readiness event fires.

Starting in Tokio 1.51.6, 1.53.3, and 1.54.0, `AsyncFd::new`, `AsyncFd::with_interest`, `AsyncFd::try_new`, and `AsyncFd::try_with_interest` are deprecated in favor of the `unsafe` constructors `AsyncFd::register` and `AsyncFd::register_with_interest`. Callers must ensure that the file descriptor remains valid, open, and unchanged for the lifetime of the `AsyncFd`.
